name: Social liberalism
summary: Social liberalism keeps the liberal commitment to individual freedom, equal rights and representative government, but holds that real freedom needs favorable social and economic conditions. It therefore backs a mixed, regulated market economy, a welfare state, progressive taxation and action against poverty, while rejecting revolutionary socialism and central planning.
scope: The new-liberal / social-liberal tradition as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's entry on liberalism describes it (the 'new', 'revisionist', 'welfare state' or 'social justice' liberalism): T. H. Green, L. T. Hobhouse (Liberalism, 1911), J. A. Hobson, Keynes and Beveridge, and the egalitarian liberalism of John Rawls that the same entry ties to it. It excludes classical and neoliberal market liberalism, and social democracy proper. Where these thinkers say nothing, the statement is null; adherents' party programmes and the 1906-14 Liberal governments are not used as the ideology's own record, because the Liberals governed as one party among others.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) attacks reserving offices and education for those of rank and the privileges of class.

abolish-income-tax.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) supports taxing incomes by a progressive super-tax and shifting taxation toward unearned wealth, not abolishing income tax.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) says religious liberty is incomplete while any belief is penalised and that no religion can be imposed from outside.

arms-reduction.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II, IX) calls for withstanding the tyranny of armaments and describes the Liberal as an opponent of swollen armaments.

ban-interest.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) lists the unavoidable payment for the use of capital among the functions mechanical Socialism wrongly denies.

bound-labor.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. I, II) counts the serf's tie to the soil and class and corporate barriers to occupation among the restraints Liberalism assails.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) says fiscal liberty means responsible government, no taxation without representation, and (ch. IX) that financial control must stay with the Commons.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) says democracy depends on the intermediate organisations linking the individual to the whole, not on direct rule over the masses.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VII) holds that morality cannot be made by compulsion and that character grows from within, so coercion cannot serve moral virtue.

central-planning.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) rejects mechanical Socialism's control of industry by government as a Utopia that gives too little scope to liberty and personal initiative, and says the state could never be the sole producer.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) argues that support as a legal right is better than charity, which makes people dependent and flows to failures.

civil-marriage.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) welcomes establishing marriage in law on a purely contractual basis and leaving its sacramental side to religion.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) distrusts tutelage as the kind given to a fattened goose, yet (ch. IX) allows that a semi-despotic colonial system may be the best safeguard where a planter oligarchy would otherwise rule.

class-collaboration.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) denies the clear-cut class war and calls for comradeship and the harmonising of capital and labour in Liberal Socialism.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) rejects mechanical Socialism's one-factor reading of history and its class war resting on a clear-cut class division that does not exist.

clerical-rule.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. I, VII) places priest-backed rule in the authoritarian stage Liberalism supersedes and separates doctrine from state control.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II, VIII) welcomes union combination so that workers bargain on terms of equality with employers.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) puts Liberalism, standing by national autonomy and international equality, in conflict with the imperial idea and criticises empire run for commercial syndicates.

conscription.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VII, IX) wants alternatives to military service for conscientious objectors and lists compulsory service imposed on a reluctant people among reactionary policies.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) founds the common good on the common will and holds that democracy rests on every grown-up person taking part in forming it.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) notes democracy is rule by majority, not by universal consent, and proposes a second chamber and referendum as brakes on a headstrong majority.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) says every citizen has a claim of right, not charity, to the material support for a healthy civilised life where the market fails to give it.

decide-locally.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) calls devolution and the revival of local government of the essence of democratic progress, while keeping national standards for industrial law.

democracy-best.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) makes democracy the necessary basis of the Liberal idea, while admitting that some liberty and justice might be better secured by a limited franchise or a good despotism.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) says any Liberal Socialism must be democratic and come from below, and rejects class war and rule imposed by a superior few.

direct-action.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) holds that popular government is won and kept through legislative and party action, and records the strike method failing in 1897.

direct-votes.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) regrets that Liberals closed the door on the referendum and would use it on rare measures of fundamental import, though not on finance.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) ties each person's reward to the function they perform, with public provision only for primary needs, not distribution by need.

distribution-by-process.rationale: The Stanford entry on liberalism reports Nozick classing Rawls's difference principle as a pattern principle that puts no weight on who produced the goods.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) lists protection and fiscal preference binding the colonies among the reactionary imperial programme, and Hobson (ch. on economic nationalism) condemns economic nationalism and closed economic blocs.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) cites martial-law executions and the suspension of ordinary guarantees of trial as the arbitrary government Liberalism attacked.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) insists on one law for government and subjects, noble and commoner, rich and poor.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) defines economic equality as equating reward with social function, not equal rewards, and the Stanford entry on liberalism reports Rawls allowing only inequalities that best serve the least advantaged.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) says race is wrongly confused with nationality and points to Canada, where French and British fused into one nation despite differences.

every-country-ready-for-democracy.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) says that where a common will and interest in public affairs definitely fails there is no case for democracy, though enfranchisement is itself a stimulus.

experts-over-public.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) says the best and wisest must carry a convinced public rather than impose laws, because no one can permanently stand irresponsible power.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) names executions without regular trial, as under martial law, among the arbitrary acts Liberalism attacked.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) supports a rapidly increasing super-tax on large incomes, which a single flat rate would exclude.

free-trade.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II, IX) holds that tariffs obstruct enterprise and create inequality and that Liberalism will always fight for free exchange, and Hobson argues the world market is expansible so one nation's gain is not another's loss.

free-trade-promotes-peace.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IV) records the Liberal case that free trade meant peace by removing national antagonisms, and Hobson argues that tariff bargaining embroils governments in traders' conflicts.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) calls a person who stands at another's caprice a slave and says a free person is controlled only by rules binding all.

gradual-change.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) concludes that progress is more continuous and secure when problems are met piecemeal by cautious experiment than by destroying everything to erect a complete system.

harm-principle.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VII) declines Mill's self-regarding distinction, holding that a person's own good concerns the community, though compulsion cannot form character, and he allows tutelage of the drunkard and feeble-minded.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) rejects official Socialism's scheme in which an Eugenist decides who may be born, as incompatible with Liberal liberty.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) makes the equation of reward with useful service the centre of Liberal economics and treats unearned income as social wealth.

independent-unions.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) welcomes the emancipation of trade unions as free combinations of workers.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The Stanford entry on liberalism describes Rawls's political liberalism as a framework neutral between controversial comprehensive doctrines, which excludes law founded on one scripture.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) treats letting municipal services fall into private hands as a source of partial monopoly, which points to public supply.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) calls mechanical Socialism's attribution of social development to the economic factor alone a false interpretation, since that factor is as much effect as cause.

minority-veto.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VII) holds that state compulsion is justified where one person's non-conformity wrecks the purpose of others, since uniformity is sometimes needed.

moral-incentives.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) says every function needs remuneration that stimulates it and that no Socialism ignoring the personal incentive could last.

municipal-businesses-mixed-economy.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VII) cites the municipal tramway running beside private buses as a legitimate form of collective action that leaves private choice open.

nation-first.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) holds that the cause of democracy is bound up with internationalism, that the world's unity must be reflected in political institutions, and that national emulation should turn from armaments to contributions to civilization.

national-self-determination.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) says Liberalism's general tendency favours autonomy, but also that a weaker nation governed under ordinary law within a larger union may fare best, so lines must follow history and practical judgment.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VII, VIII) assigns the state far more than protection, from securing conditions of self-maintenance to supervising industry and providing pensions and insurance.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) condemns monopoly values created by licensing laws and municipal services left in private hands.

one-party-rule.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) founds democracy on a common will formed by every grown-up person and holds government answerable to the community, which excludes an exclusive ruling party.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) calls the supremacy of the elected legislature a condition of democracy, though he wants a second chamber and rare referendums as checks.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) holds that democracy depends on devolution, local government and the trade union and chapel affairs that give people a say in what touches them.

party-controls-media.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) counts liberty of speech, writing and printing among the personal liberties Liberalism secures.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. I, II) treats rule from above on personal authority as the pre-Liberal stage and makes law applied impartially to all the first liberty.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) says the old doctrine of absolute sovereignty is dead and the world's unity must be reflected in political institutions, taking the empire's council as a model of the international state.

positive-liberty.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VII, VIII) holds that nominal freedom from legal restraint can impair real freedom and that liberty needs economic conditions, and the Stanford entry on Green presents the same positive-freedom case.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) calls the prevention of suffering from lack of adequate comforts the prime justification of public expenditure, and the Stanford entry on liberalism reports Rawls ranking the least advantaged first among inequalities.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) makes impartial law, independent courts and cheap accessible procedure the first condition of liberty, enforced by the community against private coercion.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) makes government by fixed rules of law, applied impartially through independent courts, the first condition of liberty.

property-fundamental.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) denies that property rights are conferred by nature, calls the basis of property social, and gives the state an overlordship over property, though he still protects the individual's earnings.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) holds that the basis of property is social and defines individual rights in terms of the common good, restoring the social conception of property.

proportional-representation.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) says Liberals will be driven to proportional representation the more they insist on a genuinely representative Commons.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) demands one impartial law for all and says there can be no question as to Liberalism's attitude to elementary rights regardless of race.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) holds that the conditions of social efficiency mark a minimum of industrial remuneration, that the living wage should cover a family and its risks, and that the state must secure it where the market does not.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II, VIII) regards combinations of capital with distrust and wants industry supervised by the state and monopoly profits recovered for the community.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VII) would substitute alternatives for conscientious objectors and gives weight to minority conviction, yet says the common conviction of the common good must in the end prevail over the individual conscience.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) holds that the advantages of the soil itself, being no one's labour, should fall to the community.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. I) describes rulers who are gods or descendants of gods as the authoritarian order Liberal government replaced.

second-chamber.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) proposes an impartial second chamber subordinate to the Commons that can send a measure to the people or a new election.

separate-church-state.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VII) approves the severance of religious worship and doctrinal teaching from the mechanism of state control and resists state doctrinal teaching.

separated-powers.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II, IX) demands an independent judiciary and a check on the Commons by a second chamber, and sees authority limited by authority in modern states.

single-common-good.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII, IX) makes the common good grounded in a common will and harmony his unifying principle, against a politics of competing interests.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) rejects change by revolutionary overturn and root-and-branch replacement in favour of piecemeal reform of existing institutions.

social-market-economy.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) keeps personal enterprise and remuneration in a market economy while the state secures a minimum through pensions, insurance and public provision.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) states that free government is government by fixed rules of law to which the ruler himself is subject.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VII) treats the community as arbiter between conflicting interests, and the Stanford entry on liberalism quotes Hobson on elected officials as representatives of the community.

state-harmful.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II, VII) argues that law and state coercion against private coercion are conditions of liberty, so there is no case for abolishing the state.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The Stanford entry on liberalism describes Rawls's political liberalism as neutral between controversial comprehensive doctrines, religious or not.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: The Stanford entry on liberalism describes Rawls's political liberalism as a framework neutral between controversial comprehensive doctrines, not one that backs ways of life the state judges good.

strong-leader.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) holds that hardly anyone is wise enough to stand irresponsible power, that leadership must win a convinced people, and that elected legislatures and fixed law constrain government.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II, IX) makes liberty of thought, speech and peaceable discussion basic and a responsible government answerable to a free electorate.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) calls the tariff an obstruction to enterprise and a source of inequality, and Hobson condemns protective and discriminative tariffs.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) says inherited wealth stands on a different footing from earned wealth and that more tax on it would be a net gain if it costs no useful function.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) endorses a rapidly increasing super-tax on large incomes and a discrimination of earned from unearned income, treating the proceeds as social wealth owed to the community.

taxation-theft.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) argues that a tax on social wealth is not robbery but repayment of what was due to society: Peter is not robbed.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II, IX) says it is of the essence of Liberalism to oppose force, that aggression is pointless in a free world, and that national emulation should not seek territory.

total-state.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) rejects official Socialism's organisation of every life by a superior few and wants the average person to have free play in personal life.

unions-good.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) calls the emancipation of trade unions a liberating movement because combination put workers on terms of equality with employers, while noting unions can also oppress.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) backs state-aided insurance for sickness and invalidity and lists care of the sick among collective responsibilities, without prescribing one public system.

vanguard-party.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) rejects Socialism directed by committees and master minds behind democratic forms, and requires any Liberal Socialism to come from below.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The Stanford entry on liberalism reports that Rawls requires a property-owning democracy with wide diffusion of ownership, whereas Hobhouse prefers state tenancy to small landlords.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) calls the extension of interest in public things a good in itself and a condition of other goods.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. II) counts the wife's capacity to hold property and conduct business on her own account among Liberalism's domestic liberties.

women-suffrage.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) treats the exclusion of a sex from the franchise as to be judged by the response it would make and notes only the Liberal party's tardiness in meeting the women's demand.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. VIII) says public provision should uniformly call on the individual for a corresponding effort and secures independence for all who do not forfeit it by idleness.

workers-councils.rationale: Hobhouse (ch. IX) holds that democracy rests on adult suffrage and the supremacy of the elected legislature, with intermediate bodies linking people to it, not replacing it.

missingStatements.text: Freedom requires that people have the material means to act on it, not only the absence of interference.
missingStatements.rationale: Hobhouse and Green hold that liberty depends on social and economic conditions, which justifies an active state.

missingStatements.text: Increases in land value created by the community should belong to the community.
missingStatements.rationale: Hobhouse treats site value as by right communal and holds that advantages of the soil itself should fall to the community.

quotes.text: this explains why Liberal opinion has fastened on the conception of site value as being by right communal and not personal property

quotes.text: all advantages that are derived from the qualities or position of the soil itself, or from the enhancement of prices by tariffs would, since they are the product of no man's labour, fall to no man's share, or, what is the same thing, they should fall to every man, that is, to the community

notes: Re-audit (rules 7). Searched: Hobhouse's full Liberalism (all chapters, by theme: liberty, economy, property, tax, wages, unions, democracy, constitution, religion, family, empire, internationalism), the Stanford entries on liberalism, Green and Rawls, Hobson's Morals of Economic Internationalism; Green's Lectures on Political Obligation and Hobson's Problems of Poverty were saved but add no answer beyond Hobhouse. Many earlier answers rested on Wikipedia or on a general liberal value and are now null. Culture-war, ecology, technology, monetary and most foreign-policy statements are not addressed by these texts. Britannica is blocked; Keynes's and Beveridge's own texts were not read in full (Beveridge's report is not on Gutenberg or the local corpora; Keynes's Treatise-era works there concern money and the peace), so their positions come only through the Stanford entry.
